speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Our intense efforts to improve rail reliability are producing results.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Reliability measured by Mean Kilometres (km) Between Failure (MKBF) shows significant and sustained improvement.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Recent surveys by the Public Transport Council (PTC) show that commuters’ perceptions of MRT services have improved.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Our MRT is now on par with other world-class systems like the Taipei Metro and Hong Kong Mass Transit Railway (MTR).

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: These improvements are the result of a concerted multi-year effort.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: It required rigorous operations and maintenance, disciplined investment and countless personal sacrifices by thousands of public transport workers who have worked day and night to improve the network.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I would also like to thank commuters for their patience and understanding.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: In particular, for the Early Closures and Late Openings (ECLOs), which have given the Land Transport Authority (LTA) and the rail operators precious engineering hours to step up maintenance and renewal as our MRT lines age.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Our efforts to improve rail reliability have, however, come at substantial expense to both the operators and the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: First, the rail operators have ramped up their operations and maintenance to support the much higher level of reliability.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Between 2016 and 2017, the total cost of running the rail network has increased by around $270 million.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: As the fares paid by commuters do not cover operating costs, the rail companies are operating at a loss.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Singapore Bus Services (SBS) Transit’s train division also lost tens of millions of dollars.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Second, the Government has spent around $1.9 billion to take over ownership of all rail operating assets.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: While the $1.9 billion is once-off, the Government is now also responsible for the proper and timely renewal of these assets, and this is a huge and continuing financial liability.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Under the rail financing framework, the Government pays for the full upfront cost of civil infrastructure and the first set of operating assets.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The subsequent operations and maintenance of operating assets are supposed to be fully paid for by the operators, through the collection of fares and non-fare revenues, such as advertising.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The depreciation cost of operating assets is supposed to be largely recovered by the Government through licence charges.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: But in practice, as fares have been inadequate to cover the cost of operations, Government subsidies have exceeded their intended scope of funding the civil infrastructure and the first set of operating assets.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: With intensified maintenance to reach the current level of reliability, the Government operating subsidies have increased further.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: So, this is nearly $1 billion a year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This will be on top of the Government spending $25 billion on civil infrastructure, to build and equip new lines.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: LTA and the rail operators are working closely to keep costs under control.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: For example, LTA is using its asset renewal programme to install new technologies, such as condition monitoring sensors.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: For new MRT lines like the Jurong Region Line, LTA is actively engaging the rail operators upstream on the design of the system, to ensure that it is designed and built with efficient downstream operations and maintenance in mind.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The rail operators are also pooling their engineering and maintenance capabilities and collaborating with ST Engineering to cut out duplication and raise productivity.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: All these upstream interventions are necessary, but they will not fully offset the higher costs of operating and maintaining a highly reliable rail network.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Members may ask: why did fares fall below operating cost?

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: PTC’s fare formula is supposed to keep fares in line with macroeconomic cost factors, such as inflation, wages, fuel costs and increases in the network capacity, with a productivity extraction.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: But until recently, the PTC fare adjustments were not fully implemented.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: If we had strictly followed PTC’s fare formula, the operators would have been better able to cover the costs of the intensified maintenance.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: As it is, the additional costs have been partly covered by increased Government subsidy and partly absorbed by the operators who have been incurring substantial losses.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: PTC’s current fare formula is valid until 2023.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We will continue to operate under this formula.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: But we must have the discipline to implement the formula fully, as we adjust fares over the next four years.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: In due course, the PTC will need to review the fare adjustment mechanism to reflect the increased operating cost to support the intensified maintenance and the additional operating subsidies from the Government to the MRT system.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The details are being worked out between the Ministry of Transport (MOT) and the Ministry of Finance.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I would just like to ask one question.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Now that we are at the sweet spot of 950,000 MKBF, does MOT strive to achieve a higher number?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The reason why I ask this is because, in life, whilst it is always good to have nicer things, ultimately, somebody needs to pay for it.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: The question is, are commuters prepared to pay at such a high level of reliability?

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: It is a little bit like the quality control chart which we studied in engineering.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: We know that once you have hit a certain sweet spot, as the Member puts it, you can still achieve higher quality control but the incremental cost required is extremely high.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: In fact, the curve is not like that of plateauing; the curve is exponential.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: It does not mean no more delays of more than five minutes, but it means that the frequency of occurrence is tolerable.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: It will not be often that you encounter such delays.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: And, if you want to achieve an even higher level of reliability, then one must be prepared to pay for more.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: My own sense is that if we can consistently maintain this one million MKBF, that should be good enough.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: But if for various reasons, future Singapore commuters are demanding an even higher level and are prepared to pay for that greater level of reliability, well, for that, we leave it to the next Transport Minister.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: But do not forget one thing, that having crossed a million, it does not mean it will always be up there.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: I am a chronic heart disease patient, and I know that I have to take the medication for life.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: My doctors are happy, I am happy, my family is happy, but it does not mean I can stop the medication.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: The moment I stop the medication, I know what will happen.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One, I agree with the Minister that having an improved MKBF does not mean that MKBF will always be at that level.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In that light, I would like to ask the Minister whether this would be a suitable time to consider introducing service quality as one of the factors in the Fare Review formula.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I say this because this will help set the bar for service quality and help to deter decline in service quality in future years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My second supplementary question is that I would like to ask the Minister: does LTA monitor the frequency of delays of less than five minutes, and if not, are there any plans to do so?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is really to enhance the commuter experience on an everyday basis.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: We track all delays, we log all delays and we analyse all delays, whether it is one minute, 30 seconds, five minutes or 10 minutes.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: That is how we are able to churn out the data.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: One major service quality is MKBF – frequency of delays – which is what we are monitoring.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: That is why we included the Network Capacity Factor, in the Fare Formula, as a proxy for crowdedness.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Minister, I understand that the current fare levels do not cover system operating cost for rail and they have not for some time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I just have two supplementary questions related to that.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: And, second, what kind of changes are we looking at to fare levels?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Do we have to expect fare levels in the longer run to reach that target level?

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: As I have said, this was before my time when there was a big public debate, resulting in the White Paper on public transport.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: The Government, and I suppose this House, reached a certain long-term view about how one should fund public transport, and it was as what I had articulated in my reply just now.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: So, we had a certain long-term view about what the operating subsidy should be; it should be zero.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: So, my more limited objective in the medium term is to be able to cover the recent level of intensified maintenance, which has cost the operators a lot of money but has delivered the current level of reliability, which seems quite satisfactory.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: I think PTC will take that into account.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: But as I said at the reply, we have just adjusted the formula last year, and we have done one round, four more rounds to go.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: I think let us keep to the formula.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: And that is why the Government is footing the bill through this temporary enhanced maintenance grant.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: But the key point is, over the next four years, let us have the discipline to implement fully the fare formula adjustments which are needed.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: But I will leave it to PTC to elaborate their case.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: I would urge Members to fully support them.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: But at the same time, bear in mind that this additional maintenance expenditure, which has to be continuously incurred, which allows us to achieve this current level of reliability, has to be paid for.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: At the end of the day, let us do not forget, as a total system, who pays for the system.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: It is people like you and me, taxpayers as well as commuters.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: The Istana does not have a printing press of money.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: The money has to come from either taxpayers or commuters.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: And we just have to find a balance – what is an appropriate level.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Over the last few months – April, May, June – we have had reports in The Straits Times about various resignations in SMRT.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister share with the House what has been the impact of this reported string of resignations on SMRT's plans towards sustained rail reliability for the long haul?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second question pertains to resignations from maintenance and engineering roles, functions which have traditionally been raised in this House as an area for improvement.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is that an issue of concern for the Ministry?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Given the maintenance and engineering resignations from within SMRT, does it constitute a significant number such that Singaporeans ought to be concerned that we start slipping in terms of the targets that the Minister has set?

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: There was a recent report, not quite by all media, but a Straits Times report.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Probably one particular journalist who reported that there was a major upcoming resignation by the Head of Trains in SMRT.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: I read it and I immediately texted the Chairman of SMRT.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: As soon as he landed at the airport, he replied to me that "it is fake news".

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: The Straits Times gave an apology, but in tiny font size.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Yes, I understand apologies usually are like that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We have had to deal with some of these as well; and it is always a small section somewhere and you wished it were larger.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Generally, the larger point, of course, is about those numbers that the same reporter I believe you are referring to has reported consistently on SMRT issues.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Thirty, I believe was the number for human resource-related resignations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And my concern is whether there is a deeper issue within SMRT that the public ought to be concerned about.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: It is a very good team of people.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister what is the MKBF for East-West Line because my constituency is in Jurong and the East-West Line is actually quite old.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, is there a plan for even individual lines to reach an MKBF of a million as it is now just an average across the country?

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: At my level, I look at the whole network.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: But yes, I also look at individual lines.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: So, it is not too difficult to track them.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: The reason, I did explain a few days ago, between North-South Line and East-West Line, both are almost 30 years old and we are changing out some of the core asset items.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: We started this process with the North-South Line, so the North-South Line benefited from this earlier renewal process.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: The North-South Line now is 1.4 million MKBF.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: The East-West Line will eventually catch up and exceed one million.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: I understand the original target subsidy level was about 0%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: The operating cost subsidy level going forward, should it be closer to 0% or 30%?

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: The fares have to be adjusted through a formula, which is what we all agreed, and having debated, discussed and settled on the formula, and the formula will last for a period, in our case, five years.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: I think much more important is to achieve that discipline.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Each time the adjustment comes out, the calculation, what is the output, stick to it.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: If you do that and if you are able to do that for four more years, including trying to see how this enhanced maintenance, which has given us today's outcome, can be better funded through additional fares, then I think we would be, in the short term, in a much more comfortable position than what we are today.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: We must never give up on this hope, but if it is not possible in the medium term, it does not matter.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: But if we can reverse it, which I think we can, if we are able to stick to the formula plus taking a look at how the enhanced resources that we have put in can be recovered, then I think, we will be home.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I checked my notes last night and at the first MOT Committee of Supply after the last General Election in April 2016, the Minister mentioned to this House that this Government will solve all the rail problems by the end of this term of Government.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I was sitting there and when I heard the Minister say it, I nearly fell off my chair.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: That night, I wrote to the Minister and I told the Minister that we have set ourselves an uphill task and I was concerned that we may have over-promised.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: So, with that in mind, Minister, can I ask, what are your thoughts between April 2016 and now, and whether going forward – I know you have said it is for the next Transport Minister to decide – maybe some goals and objectives?

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Then and now – then my hair was white, now my hair is black.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: It is not my style to over-promise because, in politics, we all know this mantra: under-promise, over-deliver.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: But, when I look at the situation at that time, and having interviewed the various stakeholders, I decided that, no, this is an occasion to break the rule and to set a stretch target in order to rally the whole troop – the tens and thousands of workers out there – towards a common goal and get them inspired.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: That is why I opted for this figure.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: It was not a million initially, in fact.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: As we go along, we found that, hey, we actually can push further.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: So, I rounded it up to a million.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: But, as I have articulated just now, having reached the million, the more important thing now is to have the discipline to ensure that the financial adjustments are made in time and, at the operational level, do not be complacent, because you can just walk backwards very easily.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Especially for the old lines, the North-South and East-West Lines, after you have renewed the core asset group, even if you do very little, they may be able to deliver a very reliable service because that is how engineering systems work.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: It is very critical that LTA and the operators and the leadership are fully aware of this.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: It does not mean that once you have achieved some level of reliability, it will always be there; you can walk backwards very quickly.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: It may not be immediate, but it will show up in a few years' time, as we experienced not too long ago.
